messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Somchai was 72 years old, a South Eastern Asian man who had spent most of his life trying to be useful, steady, and easy to live with. He had worked for years as a nanny in American households, a role that suited the way he liked to move through the world: attentive, quiet, careful not to burden anyone. He came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly on edge and worn down, with a score of 57 on the PCL-5 reflecting how much the old experience still crowded into his present life.

The event he spoke about was a period of physical abuse by a romantic partner many years earlier, but when he described it, the past felt close and immediate. He recalled being struck and overpowered in the dark, with the room itself becoming part of the fear. What stayed with him was not only what had happened, but the helpless position his body had been forced into. Even now, when he remembers it, the memory does not feel fully like his own; he says it feels as though it belongs to someone else, as if he is looking at another man’s suffering rather than his own. Yet when the memory comes, it does not stay distant for long. The terror returns with the same force he felt at the time, and he notices his body slipping back into that old posture, as though he is again pinned in the same position, unable to move or protect himself.

In the years that followed, Somchai organized his life around not having to feel that helplessness again. He had come to believe that anger was something dangerous and best kept sealed away, and he described never allowing himself to feel it, much less show it. Even when something upset him, he would swallow it down and keep his face calm. He also began to avoid circumstances that reminded him of the event, especially darkness. At home, he preferred lights left on in hallways and rooms, and if evening settled in and the house grew dim, he felt his body tense before he could reason it out. He also tried to avoid anything that might become stressful, turning down demands whenever he could and steering conversations away from conflict. Over time, this narrowed the kind of life he felt able to tolerate.

His work as a nanny made that narrowing especially difficult to hide. Caring for a child meant being around sudden movements all day, and that had become one of the moments most likely to set off his sense of danger. If a child darted around a corner, dropped a toy unexpectedly beside him, or moved quickly behind him, he would react before he had time to think, jumping as if something threatening were happening. He hated that reaction because it made him feel exposed and old, but he could not stop it. Even in familiar homes where he knew the layout well and where the family treated him kindly, he found himself unable to relax. He remained watchful during ordinary routines, sitting stiffly during quiet moments and keeping part of his attention on what might happen next. He said that even in places he knew were safe, his body did not seem to agree.

Over the weeks and months, these habits began to affect the way he lived. He avoided evening errands when he could, kept the lights on more than he used to, and tried to leave situations before they became tense. At work, he made himself appear patient and composed, but the strain of staying alert while also suppressing any sign of irritation left him drained. His marriage was not described as conflictual, but he noticed that keeping every difficult feeling locked away left him with less room to speak plainly about what he needed. He had lived for so long as the person who managed without complaint that asking for help felt foreign.

What brought Somchai to seek treatment now was the growing sense that he could no longer keep everything contained. The same old terror was coming back too vividly when the memory surfaced, and the jumps in response to sudden movement were becoming harder to hide. He was most afraid that his body would keep reacting as if danger were present even when he knew he was safe, and he hoped treatment might help him feel less trapped by the past and less afraid of ordinary moments in his own home and workplace.
